_README: Discovery + auto-tick settings for session-restore.
Nothing here names a repository. A background scan reads ~/.claude/projects/,
resolves each conversation's real working directory from its transcript, and
records it in sessions-registry.json as a PROJECT holding its CONVERSATIONS.
WHICH of them reopen is your choice -- make it with select-sessions.ps1 (or
ccs), not here. These numbers only decide what arrives PRE-TICKED.
recencyDays           a newly discovered PROJECT arrives ticked if it was
worked in within this many days.
sessionWindowDays     within a project, a newly discovered CONVERSATION
arrives ticked if it was active within this many days.
includeWorktrees      true  = git worktrees are discovered, shown as their
own lane under the parent repo, and restorable.
false = hidden entirely and never restored, including
any already recorded in the registry.
A PROJECT is a repository. Under it sit LANES: 'main'
for the repo's own tree, and one per worktree. A
worktree is a separate tree with its OWN git index, so
it gets its own lane and its own budget instead of
competing with main for one.
autoTickPerWorktree   the roll's budget for EACH worktree lane, same rules
as autoTickPerDirectory below.
autoTickPerDirectory  how many conversations in the MAIN lane the roll keeps
ticked, newest first. RECOMPUTED ON EVERY SCAN, so the
set follows the work: return to an old slice and it
re-ticks itself, move on and it falls out. Without a
ceiling a repo with sixteen live conversations would
open sixteen tabs.
Conversations you TOUCH in the picker are PINNED and
the roll never changes them -- otherwise the scan would
undo your choices within the hour. A pinned+ticked one
spends part of this ceiling, so the total stays bounded
however it was set. Press U in the picker to hand one
back to the roll.
registryWindowDays    conversations older than this are not tracked at all.
Bounds the scan: without it every historical transcript
on the machine would be read on every pass.
maxSessions           cap on tabs opened in ONE restore. The tool SAYS how
many it dropped -- it never truncates silently. Use
-All to ignore it once.
transcriptTools       how much of the machinery the reading pane shows.
Measured across six transcripts: text 50, thinking 84,
tool_use 129, tool_result 130 -- tool traffic outnumbers
prose five to one, and that ratio IS the wall of text.
folded  a run of calls becomes ONE line naming what
ran. You still know how much happened.
full    every block starts OPEN.
hidden  nothing but a count beside the speaker.
Since 2026-08-31 this sets only the DEFAULT state.
Every block folds on its own click, and an opened one
shows its result COMPLETE - it used to be the first
line, or six lines under full, which is most of why
the terminal appeared to show more than this pane.
folded IS THE CHEAP ONE, and on a slow machine it is
the single biggest lever here: a closed block builds
one summary line, and its content is constructed only
the first time you open it. full builds every block in
the conversation up front.
The 'Steps:' button in the window cycles these and
writes your choice back here, so this is a starting
value rather than somewhere you have to come.
readingWidth          how wide the reading pane sets its prose.
measured  THE DEFAULT since 2026-08-31. Caps the
line near 100 characters however wide the
window gets. An uncapped line on a
maximised pane is 120+ characters, and
tracking back to the start of the next one
is what makes a long reply tiring.
full      fill the window instead. The type no
longer scales up with it: that grew the
body to 20px on a wide pane, which is
zooming rather than scaling and was half
of 'the text is too large and too wide
spaced'. Now one fixed 13/18 either way.
'full' OVERRIDES the cap. If this file says full and
the capped measure was what you wanted, change it here
- a setting beats a default, which is the point of it.
textRendering         how glyphs are antialiased. This one is genuinely a
matter of your eyes and your monitor, which is why it
is a setting and not a decision:
grayscale  the default. No colour fringing, which is
what ClearType does to every stem on a
near-black ground.
cleartype  subpixel antialiasing -- what your browser
uses. Sharper, at the cost of that fringe.
It CANNOT be judged from a screenshot: the renderer the
tests draw through always composites greyscale, so a
captured 'cleartype' sample is greyscale wearing a
label. Flip it, look at the real window, keep whichever
you prefer. Takes effect on the next launch.
excludePatterns       PowerShell -like patterns matched against the resolved
working directory; environment variables are expanded.
The home directory is always excluded, pattern or not.
DO NOT exclude '*\.claude\worktrees\*'. It was there
briefly, on the reasoning that two sessions in one tree
share a git index -- which is backwards. A git worktree
has its OWN index; 'one worktree per lane' is the
MITIGATION for that hazard, not the hazard. Excluding
them hid a live session working in .claude/worktrees/D1
and no amount of rescanning could surface it.
A stale worktree is handled by sessionWindowDays on its
own: measured, the preserved bounded-contexts worktree
lists 22 conversations and ticks ZERO, because all of
them are older than the window. Listed, restores
nothing. Fold it away with LEFT in the picker, or untick
the project.
NONE of these gate the restore. Once a conversation is ticked, your tick wins
and it reopens; staleness is reported, never acted on. One source of truth.
Everything for this tool lives in this folder. Your selections are in
sessions-registry.json beside this file (gitignored -- the paths are local).
select-sessions.ps1            choose what reopens
restore-sessions.ps1 -DryRun   see exactly what would come back
restore-sessions.ps1 -Scan     refresh the registry now (the hourly task)
//panelScanMaxAgeSeconds: How fresh the registry has to be for the panel to skip its opening scan.
Measured with 117 conversations: the scan is 679 ms cold, 329 ms warm, out
of 1.94 s from double-click to a usable screen. An hourly task already
rescans, so re-walking every transcript because you opened the panel twice
in a minute buys nothing. When the scan IS skipped and the list is over a
minute old the panel says so in its header, so a stale list is never quiet.
R always rescans; -Scan forces one; -NoScan never scans. 0 disables the
skip and restores the old always-scan behaviour.
